Introduction:
Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is a chronic cholestatic liver disease characterized by the immune-mediated destruction of small and medium-sized intrahepatic bile ducts. The aetiology of PBC is considered to be a complex interaction between genetic and environmental factors. However, the only environmental factors in epidemiological studies that have been consistently associated with this disease are urinary tract infections [ 1–3 ] and cigarette smoking [ 1–4 ]. Although genome-wide association studies continue to identify additional genetic risk factors for this disease and recent studies have suggested clustering associated with toxic waste sites [ 5 ] and coal mines [ 6 ], few rigorously studied environmental risk factors have been identified over the last two decades.

It has been recognized for several decades that PBC prevalence varies markedly around the world. Amongst the highest reported prevalence estimates of PBC were found in the Calgary region, Canada in 2002 (227 per million population [ 7 ]), in Olmsted County, USA in 2000 (402 per million [ 8 ]), and in Northern England, UK in 1994 (335 per million population) [ 9 ], while much lower frequencies were reported in Victoria, Australia in 2013 (81 per million) [ 10 ] and in New Zealand in 2008 (99 per million) [ 11 ]. Different methods of case ascertainment and genetic factors may explain part of this variation, but the substantial differences observed among populations of shared ethics and cultural background raise the hypothesis that environmental factors influence the disease aetiology. Moreover, we previously provided strong evidence that there is a latitude gradient for PBC in Australia, with the highest prevalence in the highest latitude state of Tasmania (40–43°S) and the lowest prevalence in the lowest latitude state of Queensland (10–29°S) [ 12 ]. This finding supports the possibility that low exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation or low vitamin D levels may play some role in disease aetiology. Indeed, there is a well-established precedent with a potent latitudinal gradient and UV exposure being protective for multiple sclerosis (MS) [ 13–16 ] and also emerging evidence in other autoimmune diseases [ 17 , 18 ]. Vitamin D supplementation [ 19 ] and vitamin D levels [ 14 , 20 ] have also been found to be protective against MS risk. In this case–control study, we investigated whether high past sun exposure was associated with a reduced risk of PBC development.
Methods:
This case–control study was approved by the Austin Health Human Research Ethics Committee. All participants provided informed consent.

### Cases

All cases were diagnosed with either definite or probable PBC. Definite PBC was defined as the presence of liver histology compatible with PBC from liver biopsy findings, cholestatic liver function tests (elevation of serum alkaline phosphatase), and an anti-mitochondrial antibody titre of ≥1:40. Probable PBC was defined as patients fulfilling two of these three diagnostic criteria.

Gastroenterologists in the Australian state of Victoria were sent letters notifying them of the study and inviting them to ask their patients to participate between January 2014 and June 2014. Cases identified from the 2013 Victorian PBC prevalence study were also invited to participate [ 10 ] (overall response rate 91%). In total, 205 cases were recruited between January 2014 and October 2016 for this study and 200 were included in the final analysis. Three cases were excluded because they were not living in Victoria at the time of the study and two cases were excluded because their histology revealed features of PBC/autoimmune hepatitis overlap.

### Controls

Age- and sex-matched controls were recruited during the same time span as the cases from the electoral roll (12%) and via an advertisement in Victorian newspapers and community-based websites (88%), the latter utilized because the electoral role alone was unsuccessful for obtaining the required number of controls. Such general population controls are a well-established type for case–control studies, particularly when the cases come from disparate areas rather than single centres (e.g. hospitals) [ 21–23 ]. Potential participants from the electoral roll were sent a letter of invitation and a consent form. Participants who responded to advertisements were sent a copy of the consent form prior to the appointment being made. Subjects were screened via telephone for a history of liver disease and seven potential participants were excluded for this reason. Two hundred controls were recruited for this study. Controls were matched 1:1 to the cases based on sex and age (within a 5-year age band) and linked by their grouping identification number for statistical analysis.

### Measures

A lifetime calendar was utilized for the first sun-exposure measure. Subjects were sent a lifetime calendar prior to the interview and asked to fill in their place of residence and occupation for each year of their life. During the interview, subjects were asked how much time they spent in the sun for each of the years identified in the prefilled questionnaire for summer and winter from age 6 years until the time of the interview. Satellite data were used to estimate the average daily UV for each month for each year of life according to the latitude and longitude of the location of residence indicated on the lifetime calendar [ 24 ], which we then averaged over the 6-month summer and winter seasons at each latitude/longitude to obtain the seasonal average ambient UV. We then multiplied each seasonal average ambient UV by the self-reported time outdoors in summer/winter in each year of life and summated this over different age spans to calculate the total summer and winter UV exposures for each individual, hereafter referred to as the UV load. We did this for the following age spans: 6–10, 11–15, 16–20, 21–30, 31–40, and 41–50 years. We also examined cumulative UV loads for the following age spans: 6–25, 6–35, and 6 years to PBC diagnosis year (for controls, we used the same PBC diagnosis year as their matched case), and we examined the UV loads for the years prior to onset: 10, 5, and 3 years prior to onset. UV loads were categorized into quartiles and these categorical terms were assessed to evaluate the dose-dependency and shape of associations.

A verbal questionnaire was utilized for the second sun-exposure measure. Subjects were asked about the amount of time they would normally have spent in the sun during weekends and holidays over winter and summer by using validated questions [ 25 ]. This was performed for the age periods: 6–10, 11–15, and 16–20 years.

Skin phenotype was assessed by using a handheld Minolta 508 spectrophotometer at the upper inner arm and buttock—body sites that are not usually exposed to sunlight. The cutaneous melanin density was estimated by using the skin reflectance of light centred at 400 and 420 nm [ 26 ]. The standardized questionnaire also included questions pertaining to the individual’s response to sun exposure, including the number of moles and the total number of lifetime episodes of sunburn.

The questionnaire included the presenting symptoms at diagnosis of PBC, country of birth, ethnicity, educational level, history of vitamin D supplementation (before diagnosis), history of urinary tract infection (if yes, the number of urinary tract infections and at what age), history of tobacco consumption (ever smoked, ex-smoker, current smoker), other medical comorbidities, and personal and family history of liver disease and autoimmune diseases. The questionnaire also included exposure to industrial chemicals and environmental hazards.

### Statistical methods

Differences in categorical cohort characteristics between cases and controls were evaluated by using a chi-square test, while differences in continuous variables between cases and controls were evaluated by using a t -test.

The associations of covariates with case status were evaluated by using conditional logistic regression, with matched cases and controls linked by their grouping identification number, estimating an odds ratio (OR). Adjusted models were first adjusted for country of residence, education, vitamin D supplement use, and smoking; secondary adjusted models were further adjusted for the melanin density of the buttock. For the measures of UV load, for each age span, those who had already been diagnosed with PBC were excluded from that age span to ensure that exposures were prior to disease onset.
Results:
Overall, 91% of the cases were female and the mean age was 63.6 years for cases ( Table 1 ). The mean age of PBC diagnosis was 49.9 years (11.8 SD, range 20–78 years). The most common presenting symptom was fatigue (52.5%), followed by pruritus in 37%, myalgia in 27%, and right-sided abdominal pain in one-quarter of cases. Diagnosis of PBC was made through positive anti-mitochondrial antibody and cholestatic liver function tests in 60% of cases ( n = 120); the remaining cases were diagnosed through cholestatic liver function tests and liver biopsy ( n = 55, 27.5%) or based on the results of liver biopsy and cholestatic liver function tests ( n = 25, 12.5%).

As would be expected given the matching, there were no significant differences between cases and controls in either age or sex ( Table 1 ). Cases were more likely to have been born outside of Australia ( P < .001), to have a lower level of education ( P < .001), and to be smokers ( P = .065 and P = .002 for ex-smokers and current smokers, respectively). Ethnicity and body mass index did not differ by case status.

### Sun exposure prior to disease onset

Increasing time in the sun ( Fig. 1 , Supplementary Table S1 , and Supplementary Fig. S1 ) and UV load ( Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table S2 ) were associated with lower odds of being a case for all 5-year age periods from 6 to 35 years old, robust to adjustment for birthplace, education level, smoking, and buttock melanin density. The associations were consistently stronger for summer than for winter ( Fig. 2 ).

When we repeated the analysis for time in the sun by using the questionnaire method, we observed similar statistically significant associations to the calendar measures for ages 6–10 years with >4 hours in the sun [OR = 0.36, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.19, 0.57], 11–15 years (OR = 0.48, 95% CI: 0.27, 0.85), and 16–20 years (OR = 0.41, 95% CI: 0.22, 0.74), with associations again stronger for summer than for winter ( Supplementary Table S3 ).

We next examined the cumulative UV loads by adding additional 5-year periods and UV loads for particular years prior to the age of diagnosis ( Fig. 3 and Table 2 ). We found significant associations for cumulative summer UV loads of 6–25 years (OR 0.35, 95% CI: 0.19, 0.66) and 6–35 years (OR 0.4, 95% CI: 0.21,0.76). The association for cumulative summer UV load from age 6 years to the age of diagnosis was, however, not significant (OR = 0.69, 95% CI: 0.33–1.38). Again, summer associations were stronger than those of winter ( Fig. 3 ).

### Skin phenotype, history of sunburn, and number of moles

Those with a higher melanin density had lower odds of being a case ( Table 3 ). Those who had had a greater number of lifetime sunburns had lower odds of being a case, but, when this was adjusted for buttock melanin density, this was no longer significant. There was no significant relationship between number of moles and PBC ( Table 3 ).
Discussion:
We previously demonstrated a latitudinal gradient in the prevalence of PBC in Australia. In this current study, we found, for the first time, that higher levels of sun exposure and UV load prior to onset were associated with a lower risk of PBC. The association was consistently found, regardless of whether exposure was measured by using calendar or questionnaire. The relationship was stronger for summer sun than for winter sun, and exposure seemed important across a wide age span because the cumulative UV load was significant when 5-year periods were added from ages 6–10 years up to age 35 years, with higher UV loads prior to PBC diagnosis (10, 5, and 3 years) also associated with lower PBC risk.

Our findings are consistent with the hypothesis that exposure to UV may be protective for PBC. There is a large body of evidence suggesting that reduced exposure to UV is linked to the development of several other autoimmune diseases, including type I diabetes mellitus [ 27 ], Crohn’s disease [ 28 ], rheumatoid arthritis [ 29 ], and MS [ 13 , 30 ]. The body produces vitamin D under the influence of UV, and biologically active vitamin D directly and indirectly regulates the expression of >200 genes, including those that play a role in immunomodulation [ 31 ]. Therefore, reduced exposure to UV and subsequent vitamin D deficiency could explain the increased risk of PBC. There is also emerging evidence of an association with vitamin D receptor polymorphisms in PBC populations in Italy [ 32 ], Poland [ 33 ], Japan [ 32 ], and China [ 34 ]. In MS, both higher recent or lifetime sun exposure and higher serum 25(OH)D levels have been shown to be independently associated with a reduced risk of a first demyelinating event [ 14 ]. As we had prevalent cases, we were unable to assess the association between lifetime serum vitamin D levels and PBC risk, as the data were collected after PBC diagnosis.

There are also several mechanisms by which UV exposure, independently of vitamin D production, can attenuate immune responses. UV can lead to cytokine signalling alterations that can exert systemic immunosuppression [ 35 , 36 ]. It also suppresses melatonin secretion [ 37 ], which appears to have an anti-Th-1 response, i.e. decreased release of cytokines such as interferon-gamma [ 38 ]. In a mouse model of PBC, interferon-gamma had a crucial role in the early events involved in pathogenesis [ 39 ].

We found that the associations of UV load with the odds of developing PBC were stronger for summer than for winter. This could be due to the fact that summer sun, and hence UV exposure, is more important than winter sun exposure for maintaining vitamin D stores throughout the year [ 40 ]. Summer sun exposure was also found to have a greater impact on MS risk when compared with winter sun exposure in a large case–control study of MS in the USA [ 30 ]. Cumulative UV-load measures (i.e. 6–25, 6–35 years) were significantly associated with PBC risk, although the association was diminished when we assessed the cumulative UV load from age 6 years through to the age of diagnosis. We hypothesize that the most critical period for PBC risk in terms of reduced sun exposure is in adolescence and early adulthood, as has been seen in the MS literature [ 13 ], thus explaining the diminished effect seen with cumulative UV load. It is important to acknowledge that the date of diagnosis is not necessarily indicative of the date of PBC onset, especially due to the large percentage of patients who were asymptomatic at diagnosis; however, this is the best measure by which to estimate disease onset.

Two strengths of our study are that the demographic characteristics of our case cohort were similar to those of other PBC cohorts in Europe and the USA [ 7 , 41 ] and that we had a high participation rate (91%). We therefore believe that our case population is representative of the PBC population. Our controls were matched on age and sex, obtained from the same geographical location as the cases, and there were no statistically significant differences in ethnicity compared with cases. An additional strength of our study was that satellite data were used to estimate the UV load according to the latitude and longitude of each location of residence described in the calendar, therefore ensuring that the UV load was determined for each specific geographical location of residence, over each participant’s lifetime. A potential limitation of our study was that the controls were more likely to have been Australian-born; however, when a sensitivity analysis was performed by using only Australian-born participants, the associations persisted ( Supplementary Table 3 ). Controls were excluded if they had a current or past history of liver disease. However, the control group was obtained from a variety of sources due to the difficulty of obtaining controls from the Victorian electoral role. Control recruitment has become more difficult over the years due to changing privacy laws and decreased response rates to invitations to participate in studies [ 42 ], so selection bias cannot be excluded. Another potential concern is the accuracy of the recollection of sun exposure over a long period of time, but the questionnaire and calendar methods used have been well validated and shown to be reproducible [ 25 , 43 , 44 ]; also, if the accuracy of recall was a concern, then this would have applied both to controls and to cases. Two separate methods were used to obtain sun-exposure data: a lifetime calendar method and a validated time-in-sun questionnaire; both methods yielded concordant responses, thus indicating consistency in the recall of sun-exposure behaviours. While recall bias is a potential concern in prevalent case–control studies, there is no knowledge in the PBC literature that sun exposure might be associated with PBC and it thus unlikely that this would have affected the responses. We ensured that the sun exposure was assessed only ‘prior’ to disease onset, thus avoiding reverse causality as an explanation for the observed associations. We showed consistent results between the reported time in the sun and UV-load analyses, providing internal consistency and supporting a true association. Despite that, some aspects of UV exposure were too complex to take into account, such as the time of day of exposure, the amount of clothing or sunscreen worn, and the amount of cloud cover present. We also did not capture the lifetime vitamin D supplementation.

In conclusion, we have demonstrated for the first time that higher sun exposure, particularly in summer, is associated with a reduced risk of PBC, which is consistent with insufficient UV or vitamin D influencing the development of PBC. This finding requires substantiation by replication in other PBC populations, preferably using a cohort design, but provides a potential key to unlock the aetiological mysteries of this disease.
